1.title: My profile
1.desc: Your own page — who you are signed in as, the finance forms you have filed and where each one stands, your open follow-ups, loaners you checked out, and the quick actions (password, manual, favourites) without digging through menus.

1.title: Ask Healthspan
1.desc: Ask Healthspan as a full page: your saved chats on the left, the conversation on the right. Same brain as the side chat — stock, sales, accounts, targets, in plain language.

1.title: New order
1.desc: Take an order: searchable account and product pickers, deal pricing (the +1 lines add themselves), FOC lines, credit and approval checks, an HS number on submit.

1.title: Orders
1.desc: The register of every HQ order — status, amount, paid and balance, shipment marks — with a full page per order.

1.title: Log a visit
1.desc: For the product specialists, from the iPad: log every doctor/clinic visit in ~10 seconds — even when there’s no order. Pick your name once and it’s remembered.

1.title: Follow-ups & planned visits
1.desc: The team’s to-do list, generated by the visit log: every visit whose outcome was Follow-up needed stays here until ticked done, and every visit logged with a future date shows as a planned visit (overdue ones flagged). Specialists see their own; managers and admins see everyone’s.

1.title: Sales overview
1.desc: Use External only / Incl. Remedy in the toolbar to switch the whole page between third-party sales and everything.

1.title: Sales vs target
1.desc: External sales only — Remedy and Healthspan-internal orders never count toward a target. Actual booked sales versus the monthly targets set in the sheet’s Targets tab — total, per line, and per product.

1.title: Sales per specialist
1.desc: Each product specialist’s booked sales — revenue and units — over an adjustable period, and against their monthly target if one is set. Specialists are read from the order’s first tag in Shopify (e.

1.title: Leaderboard & pace
1.desc: The month-to-date race and the finish-line projection. Pace = what you’ve booked ÷ how much of the month has passed, against your target — green means on pace for 100%.

1.title: Reorder due
1.desc: Accounts past their usual buying rhythm. The cycle is learned from each account’s own order history (median gap between orders, 3+ orders needed).

1.title: Pipeline
1.desc: The funnel, staged: lead → contacted → qualified → active. Stages start from real behavior and every manual move is audited.

1.title: Events calendar
1.desc: One calendar for the room: campaigns, demos, trainings, and planned visits in a single month grid — Mench’s weekly Calendar of Events, live. Specialists see their own visits; everyone sees campaigns.

1.title: Quotations
1.desc: Formal quotations for clinics: build a quote with the same pricing as an order, print it, mark it sent/accepted/lost, and convert an accepted quote to an order in one tap. Win rate is tracked from outcomes.

1.title: Deals vs à la carte
1.desc: Do the bundles outsell single-unit pricing? Per product: units and revenue moved through deals versus à la carte, the effective per-unit price inside a deal (revenue ÷ all units including the +1), and the effective discount versus the à-la-carte price.

1.title: Free items
1.desc: Items given away at ₱0 outside any deal — samples, marketing, goodwill — kept separate from sales. Deal +1s are not here; they count as deal units.

1.title: CRM activity
1.desc: The field effort itself, per specialist: visits, calls, demos, accounts touched, and how often a contact ends in an order — from the in-app visit log. Sales activity is the input; the Sales views measure the output.

1.title: Field coverage
1.desc: Veeva-style field activity per specialist, built from bookings: how many accounts each specialist reached in the period vs their own account universe (≈6 months), orders per active day, samples given, and — most useful — the accounts not reached list, sorted by value, as a ready follow-up sheet. A booking counts as contact; visits without an order would need a call log (phase 2).

1.title: Business review
1.desc: The monthly sales performance report, built from HQ instead of typed into slides: brands, products, machines, accounts, buying behaviour and each specialist, with what HQ noticed in the numbers. People add only the commentary — the sales manager owns the wins / challenges / plan boxes, each specialist owns their own — and every box shows what it said last time.

1.title: Reports
1.desc: Every review deck for the month, built from live figures the moment you click: the team deck for the sales manager, one deck per specialist, PowerPoint or PDF. The Inputs column says whose commentary is in before anyone downloads.

1.title: Saved reports
1.desc: Your own reports, the way NetSuite people mean it: pick a source (stock, batches, sales lines, HQ orders, accounts, visits, quotes, payments, POs, finance forms, serials, loaners), tick columns, add filters, group and total, sort — and save it. Run it any time, export the CSV, or schedule it daily / weekly / monthly: at 6am Manila the server runs it as you and drops the CSV in HQ with a bell notification.

1.title: Complaints log
1.desc: Product quality reports with the batch on record — one tap into the recall trace shows every other clinic that received the same lot. Closing a complaint requires a resolution note; the log is the compliance record.

1.title: Pull-out requests
1.desc: Inventory pull-outs — stock leaving the warehouse for internal use (KOL engagements, campaigns, FOC promos, trade partnerships, launches and training) charged to a department’s fund source. Anyone can file a request; the fund source named on it approves.

1.title: Voucher for approval
1.desc: Voucher for approval — one of the finance forms. Anyone signed in can file one; it then moves through the approval steps set for that form (Admin → Approval routes), and every decision is recorded with who and when.

1.title: Request to order / pay
1.desc: Request to order / pay — one of the finance forms. Anyone signed in can file one; it then moves through the approval steps set for that form (Admin → Approval routes), and every decision is recorded with who and when.

1.title: Proof of payment

1.title: Request for replenishment
1.desc: Request for replenishment — one of the finance forms. Anyone signed in can file one; it then moves through the approval steps set for that form (Admin → Approval routes), and every decision is recorded with who and when.

1.title: Expense report (revolving fund)
1.desc: Expense report — the liquidation of a revolving fund. Whoever holds a fund itemises every peso spent in the period, receipt by receipt, and it routes to the approver set for this form (Admin → Approval routes).

1.title: Expense reimbursement

2.title: Remedy branch shipments
2.desc: A log of product Healthspan has shipped to Remedy’s clinic branches — BGC, Vertis North, Greenhills — from 2025 onward. Remedy is a sister company and a customer.

2.title: Remedy branch expiry watch
2.desc: For each Remedy branch, the stock Healthspan shipped there sorted by expiry — so each clinic can see what to use up first.

2.title: Cycle counts
2.desc: Cycle counts: pick a scope, count physically (blind — expected quantities are hidden), and the session grades itself against the stock truth. Two matching counts in a row are the evidence that lets the ledger replace the sheet.

2.title: Quarantine & disposal
2.desc: The compliance trail for stock that can’t be sold: expiring, damaged, QA-hold, and doubtful returned units sit here, out of sellable stock and ATP, until someone inspects them — release puts them back in the ledger, dispose closes the record with who and when.

2.title: Short-dated stock
2.desc: The worklist for stock that is running out of shelf life: every batch with units on hand expiring within six months, worst first, with the peso value at risk. Each lot gets a plan — discount it, give it as FOC to a loyal account, transfer it to a Remedy branch, quarantine it, or accept the write-off — an owner, and a target date, so expiring money is worked instead of watched.

2.title: Warehouse KPIs
2.desc: The warehouse scoreboard: order cycle time (taken → fulfilled), share fulfilled within 48 hours, fill rate (orders that never hit a backorder), the open queue, and units picked this week.

2.title: Purchase orders
2.desc: Purchase orders and receiving. Draft the PO, add lines, mark it ordered; when stock arrives, receive per line — batch and expiry captured at the door, written straight into the stock ledger.

2.title: Receiving
2.desc: Inbound shipments from suppliers, one record per delivery against a PO: carrier, tracking, ETD/ETA, customs, broker; the count at the door per line (batch, expiry, bin, QA hold) that writes the stock ledger and the PO; the supplier’s terms turned into a payment due date; and the landed-cost calculator — invoice × FX plus freight, insurance, duty, VAT (recoverable by default), brokerage, arrastre, storage, trucking, bank charges — allocated to a real ₱ cost per unit and applied to the PO for valuation. Short or over counts raise a claim with the supplier in one tap.

2.title: Suppliers & imports
2.desc: The supplier master: currencies, payment terms, lead times, contacts — plus every PO on the water with its ETD, ETA, and customs status in one list.

2.title: Transfer orders
2.desc: Remedy branch shipments as proper documents: draft the lines, dispatch (each line leaves the ledger as a FEFO batch-stamped movement, ref TR-n), mark delivered. In-transit units are visible instead of living in chat threads.

2.title: Serial numbers
2.desc: One row per physical equipment unit — lasers, devices, handpieces — tracked by serial number from receiving through loan, sale or disposal. Consumables stay batch-tracked; serials are for the units where which exact machine matters.

2.title: Demo / loaner units
2.desc: Demo and loaner equipment out with clinics: who has which serial, since when, due back when. Overdue loans ping whoever checked the unit out.

2.title: Batch recall trace
2.desc: The one-bad-day feature: enter a SKU and/or batch number and get every clinic that ever received it — dates, quantities, order refs — as a printable contact list. Sources: every OUT-sheet shipment row plus the platform ledger.

2.title: AR aging — receivables
2.desc: Who owes what, and for how long: every unpaid balance bucketed into current / 31–60 / 61–90 / 90+ days, per account. Ages count from the order date plus any terms noted on the order (e.

2.title: PDC register
2.desc: Every post-dated cheque, tracked to maturity: who issued it, which bank, how much, and when it can be deposited. Highlighted rows are due — deposit them.

2.title: Cash-flow forecast
2.desc: Expected collections, week by week: receivables land in the week their payment terms mature, post-dated cheques in the week they can be deposited. Overdue money gets its own bucket.

2.title: Returns & credit memos
2.desc: Returns and credit memos with permanent CM numbers. Record what came back, whether it restocks or gets written off, and print the CM for accounting.

2.title: Commissions
2.desc: Finance computes incentives here instead of by hand — on external sales only, never on Remedy or Healthspan-internal orders: per specialist, booked vs target, the rate tier reached, and the commission — any month, exportable as the payroll input. Rate tiers are editable (finance/admin) and every change is audited.

2.title: Aged inventory
2.desc: Products that haven’t sold in a while, grouped into aging, slow, and dead stock — candidates for a promo or clear-out.

2.title: Shrinkage tracker
2.desc: Flags gaps between what was received/sold and what’s actually on hand — possible loss, miscounts, or unrecorded movement.

2.title: Cash in expiring stock
2.desc: The peso value tied up in stock that’s expiring soon, bucketed by urgency.

2.title: Dashboard
2.desc: Your at-a-glance overview — total stock, what’s running out, what’s expiring, and value by product line. A good place to start each day.

2.title: Action center
2.desc: Your daily to-do in one place — what to order now, what to promo or move before it expires, what to review, and dead stock to clear. Pulls together the whole app so nobody has to hunt across tabs.

2.title: All SKUs
2.desc: Every product in one searchable table. Filter by line or category and click any row for full detail.

2.title: Batch view
2.desc: Every batch in FEFO order (first to expire, first out) — the sequence to pull stock in.

2.title: Item master
2.desc: The item master — products, prices, costs, and barcodes owned in-app. While in shadow mode, Shopify still prices the app; use this page to fix drift (⚠ rows) and add costs, then declare pricing independence on the Cutover switches page.

2.title: Product registrations
2.desc: CPR/FDA product registrations per SKU with expiry dates — expired and expiring-soon registrations float to the top so renewals never slip.

2.title: Out of stock
2.desc: Products that have hit zero stock — these need reordering now.

2.title: Low stock
2.desc: Products with fewer than 10 units left — running thin.

2.title: Negative stock
2.desc: Products showing negative stock, which usually points to a miscount or data slip worth checking.

2.title: Expiry tracker
2.desc: Batches sorted by expiry date, soonest first. Use it to decide what to sell or use up before it expires.

2.title: Reorder alerts
2.desc: Products that have dropped below their reorder point (or a threshold you set) and should be reordered.

2.title: Stockout forecast
2.desc: Predicts when each product will run out, using recent sales trend and seasonality. Order the red ones first.

2.title: Stock coverage
2.desc: How much runway you have — weeks or months of stock left at the current sales pace, per product. The chart groups SKUs from critically low to overstocked; the list ranks them lowest-cover first.

2.title: Reorder plan
2.desc: Turns the forecast into a shopping list — how much to order of each item and the estimated cost. Adjust lead time and coverage up top, then export a draft PO.

2.title: Reorder point
2.desc: The “buy-again” level for each product, based on how fast it sells and how erratic demand is. Stock at or below the reorder point means it’s time to order.

2.title: Demand variability
2.desc: Sorts products into steady, variable, and lumpy by how consistent their sales are — so you know which forecasts to trust and which need a human eye.

2.title: ABC analysis
2.desc: Ranks products by how much of your sales value they drive. A-items are the vital few to watch and count most closely.

2.title: Write-off forecast
2.desc: Estimates how much stock will expire unsold at the current pace, and the peso value at risk. Tackle the biggest ones first.

2.title: Forecast accuracy
2.desc: The honest test of the forecast: at the start of each month the model’s prediction per SKU is frozen; a month later it’s scored against what actually moved. MAPE = average % miss per SKU.

2.title: Campaign calendar
2.desc: Planned promos and campaigns as a demand signal. Anything added here shows as a banner on the stockout forecast and feeds the AI planning review, so a "10+8 anniversary promo" stops being a forecast surprise.

2.title: Promotions
2.desc: Promotions as configuration instead of free-typed deal lines: define a mechanic (buy-N-get-M free, or % off), a validity window, and the eligible SKUs — order entry applies it automatically while the promo is live.

2.title: AI planning review
2.desc: Demand planning AI: walks every SKU (stock, velocity, days-to-stockout, expiry) plus the campaign calendar and recent forecast misses, then reports the exceptions — stockout risks, expiry money, and 5 prioritized actions. An analyst, not an oracle: sanity-check quantities before ordering.

2.title: What-if simulator
2.desc: Play out a scenario — change demand or delay the next shipment — and see the effect on stockouts, write-offs, and spend.

2.title: Promo rescue simulator
2.desc: Tests whether discounting near-expiry stock pays off: set how much faster a promo sells and the discount offered, and see write-off avoided versus margin given up.

2.title: Budget optimizer
2.desc: Given a set purchasing budget, it chooses what to order first to prevent the most stockouts — urgent and high-value items lead.

2.title: Service-level simulator
2.desc: Shows the trade-off between service level and cash: a higher target means fewer stockouts but more money parked in safety stock.

2.title: Campaign surge simulator
2.desc: Model a campaign that spikes demand for a product line, and see which items would run out and how much to pre-buy.

2.title: Monte Carlo stockout risk
2.desc: Rather than a single guess, it simulates each product’s demand hundreds of times to give a probability of stocking out — accounting for how unpredictable each one is.

2.title: 12-month projection
2.desc: A 12-month forecast for one product: projected demand, a declining stock line showing when it runs out, and a confidence band around it.

2.title: Cash-flow timeline
2.desc: Projects inventory cash over six months — restocking spend versus sales coming in — so you can see when cash is most tied up.

2.title: Bulk-buy trade-off
2.desc: Checks whether a volume discount is worth it: weighs the savings against extra holding cost and the risk of stock expiring before it sells.

2.title: Remedy branch rebalancing
2.desc: Suggests moving stock between Remedy’s branches (BGC, Vertis North, Greenhills) to balance each site’s share and use up near-expiry stock. Remedy is a sister company and a customer; this is based on what Healthspan has shipped to them.

2.title: Data health
2.desc: A completeness check on the data behind every forecast — SKUs missing a price, expiry, batch, or bin, negative stock, and items with too little sales history. Fixing these in the source sheet sharpens the whole app.

2.title: Monthly movement
2.desc: Units received versus sold each month over the past year — the pulse of what’s coming in and going out.

2.title: Inventory value
2.desc: Where your inventory money sits, broken down by product line.

2.title: Deal scenarios
2.desc: What the current stock is worth if everything sells à la carte versus through the bundle deals (2+1 up to 6+1, where the +1 is free). Prices are live from Shopify where connected (sheet price otherwise).

6.desc: Turns the forecast into a shopping list — how much to order of each item and the estimated cost. Adjust lead time and coverage up top, then export a draft PO.

6.title: Write-off forecast
6.desc: Estimates how much stock will expire unsold at the current pace, and the peso value at risk. Tackle the biggest ones first.

6.title: Forecast accuracy
6.desc: The honest test of the forecast: at the start of each month the model’s prediction per SKU is frozen; a month later it’s scored against what actually moved. MAPE = average % miss per SKU.

6.title: Campaign calendar
6.desc: Planned promos and campaigns as a demand signal. Anything added here shows as a banner on the stockout forecast and feeds the AI planning review, so a "10+8 anniversary promo" stops being a forecast surprise.

6.title: Promotions
6.desc: Promotions as configuration instead of free-typed deal lines: define a mechanic (buy-N-get-M free, or % off), a validity window, and the eligible SKUs — order entry applies it automatically while the promo is live.

6.title: AI planning review
6.desc: Demand planning AI: walks every SKU (stock, velocity, days-to-stockout, expiry) plus the campaign calendar and recent forecast misses, then reports the exceptions — stockout risks, expiry money, and 5 prioritized actions. An analyst, not an oracle: sanity-check quantities before ordering.

6.title: What-if simulator
6.desc: Play out a scenario — change demand or delay the next shipment — and see the effect on stockouts, write-offs, and spend.

6.title: Promo rescue simulator
6.desc: Tests whether discounting near-expiry stock pays off: set how much faster a promo sells and the discount offered, and see write-off avoided versus margin given up.

6.title: Budget optimizer
6.desc: Given a set purchasing budget, it chooses what to order first to prevent the most stockouts — urgent and high-value items lead.

6.title: Service-level simulator
6.desc: Shows the trade-off between service level and cash: a higher target means fewer stockouts but more money parked in safety stock.

6.title: Campaign surge simulator
6.desc: Model a campaign that spikes demand for a product line, and see which items would run out and how much to pre-buy.

6.title: Monte Carlo stockout risk
6.desc: Rather than a single guess, it simulates each product’s demand hundreds of times to give a probability of stocking out — accounting for how unpredictable each one is.

6.title: 12-month projection
6.desc: A 12-month forecast for one product: projected demand, a declining stock line showing when it runs out, and a confidence band around it.

6.title: Cash-flow timeline
6.desc: Projects inventory cash over six months — restocking spend versus sales coming in — so you can see when cash is most tied up.

6.title: Bulk-buy trade-off
6.desc: Checks whether a volume discount is worth it: weighs the savings against extra holding cost and the risk of stock expiring before it sells.

6.title: Monthly movement
6.desc: Units received versus sold each month over the past year — the pulse of what’s coming in and going out.

6.title: Inventory value
6.desc: Where your inventory money sits, broken down by product line.

6.title: Deal scenarios

7.title: Write-off forecast
7.desc: Estimates how much stock will expire unsold at the current pace, and the peso value at risk. Tackle the biggest ones first.

7.title: Forecast accuracy
7.desc: The honest test of the forecast: at the start of each month the model’s prediction per SKU is frozen; a month later it’s scored against what actually moved. MAPE = average % miss per SKU.

7.title: Campaign calendar
7.desc: Planned promos and campaigns as a demand signal. Anything added here shows as a banner on the stockout forecast and feeds the AI planning review, so a "10+8 anniversary promo" stops being a forecast surprise.

7.title: Promotions
7.desc: Promotions as configuration instead of free-typed deal lines: define a mechanic (buy-N-get-M free, or % off), a validity window, and the eligible SKUs — order entry applies it automatically while the promo is live.

7.title: AI planning review
7.desc: Demand planning AI: walks every SKU (stock, velocity, days-to-stockout, expiry) plus the campaign calendar and recent forecast misses, then reports the exceptions — stockout risks, expiry money, and 5 prioritized actions. An analyst, not an oracle: sanity-check quantities before ordering.

7.title: What-if simulator
7.desc: Play out a scenario — change demand or delay the next shipment — and see the effect on stockouts, write-offs, and spend.

7.title: Promo rescue simulator
7.desc: Tests whether discounting near-expiry stock pays off: set how much faster a promo sells and the discount offered, and see write-off avoided versus margin given up.

7.title: Budget optimizer
7.desc: Given a set purchasing budget, it chooses what to order first to prevent the most stockouts — urgent and high-value items lead.

7.title: Service-level simulator
7.desc: Shows the trade-off between service level and cash: a higher target means fewer stockouts but more money parked in safety stock.

7.title: Campaign surge simulator
7.desc: Model a campaign that spikes demand for a product line, and see which items would run out and how much to pre-buy.

7.title: Monte Carlo stockout risk
7.desc: Rather than a single guess, it simulates each product’s demand hundreds of times to give a probability of stocking out — accounting for how unpredictable each one is.

7.title: 12-month projection
7.desc: A 12-month forecast for one product: projected demand, a declining stock line showing when it runs out, and a confidence band around it.

7.title: Cash-flow timeline
7.desc: Projects inventory cash over six months — restocking spend versus sales coming in — so you can see when cash is most tied up.

7.title: Bulk-buy trade-off
7.desc: Checks whether a volume discount is worth it: weighs the savings against extra holding cost and the risk of stock expiring before it sells.

7.title: Remedy branch rebalancing
7.desc: Suggests moving stock between Remedy’s branches (BGC, Vertis North, Greenhills) to balance each site’s share and use up near-expiry stock. Remedy is a sister company and a customer; this is based on what Healthspan has shipped to them.

7.title: Monthly movement

9.desc: The item master — products, prices, costs, and barcodes owned in-app. While in shadow mode, Shopify still prices the app; use this page to fix drift (⚠ rows) and add costs, then declare pricing independence on the Cutover switches page.

9.title: Product registrations
9.desc: CPR/FDA product registrations per SKU with expiry dates — expired and expiring-soon registrations float to the top so renewals never slip.

9.title: Out of stock
9.desc: Products that have hit zero stock — these need reordering now.

9.title: Low stock
9.desc: Products with fewer than 10 units left — running thin.

9.title: Negative stock
9.desc: Products showing negative stock, which usually points to a miscount or data slip worth checking.

9.title: Expiry tracker
9.desc: Batches sorted by expiry date, soonest first. Use it to decide what to sell or use up before it expires.

9.title: Reorder alerts
9.desc: Products that have dropped below their reorder point (or a threshold you set) and should be reordered.

9.title: Stockout forecast
9.desc: Predicts when each product will run out, using recent sales trend and seasonality. Order the red ones first.

9.title: Stock coverage
9.desc: How much runway you have — weeks or months of stock left at the current sales pace, per product. The chart groups SKUs from critically low to overstocked; the list ranks them lowest-cover first.

9.title: Reorder plan
9.desc: Turns the forecast into a shopping list — how much to order of each item and the estimated cost. Adjust lead time and coverage up top, then export a draft PO.

9.title: Reorder point
9.desc: The “buy-again” level for each product, based on how fast it sells and how erratic demand is. Stock at or below the reorder point means it’s time to order.

9.title: Demand variability
9.desc: Sorts products into steady, variable, and lumpy by how consistent their sales are — so you know which forecasts to trust and which need a human eye.

9.title: ABC analysis
9.desc: Ranks products by how much of your sales value they drive. A-items are the vital few to watch and count most closely.

9.title: Write-off forecast
9.desc: Estimates how much stock will expire unsold at the current pace, and the peso value at risk. Tackle the biggest ones first.

9.title: Forecast accuracy
9.desc: The honest test of the forecast: at the start of each month the model’s prediction per SKU is frozen; a month later it’s scored against what actually moved. MAPE = average % miss per SKU.

9.title: Campaign calendar
9.desc: Planned promos and campaigns as a demand signal. Anything added here shows as a banner on the stockout forecast and feeds the AI planning review, so a "10+8 anniversary promo" stops being a forecast surprise.

9.title: Promotions
9.desc: Promotions as configuration instead of free-typed deal lines: define a mechanic (buy-N-get-M free, or % off), a validity window, and the eligible SKUs — order entry applies it automatically while the promo is live.

9.title: AI planning review
9.desc: Demand planning AI: walks every SKU (stock, velocity, days-to-stockout, expiry) plus the campaign calendar and recent forecast misses, then reports the exceptions — stockout risks, expiry money, and 5 prioritized actions. An analyst, not an oracle: sanity-check quantities before ordering.

9.title: What-if simulator
9.desc: Play out a scenario — change demand or delay the next shipment — and see the effect on stockouts, write-offs, and spend.

9.title: Promo rescue simulator
9.desc: Tests whether discounting near-expiry stock pays off: set how much faster a promo sells and the discount offered, and see write-off avoided versus margin given up.

9.title: Budget optimizer
9.desc: Given a set purchasing budget, it chooses what to order first to prevent the most stockouts — urgent and high-value items lead.

9.title: Service-level simulator
9.desc: Shows the trade-off between service level and cash: a higher target means fewer stockouts but more money parked in safety stock.

9.title: Campaign surge simulator
9.desc: Model a campaign that spikes demand for a product line, and see which items would run out and how much to pre-buy.

9.title: Monte Carlo stockout risk
9.desc: Rather than a single guess, it simulates each product’s demand hundreds of times to give a probability of stocking out — accounting for how unpredictable each one is.

9.title: 12-month projection
9.desc: A 12-month forecast for one product: projected demand, a declining stock line showing when it runs out, and a confidence band around it.

9.title: Cash-flow timeline
9.desc: Projects inventory cash over six months — restocking spend versus sales coming in — so you can see when cash is most tied up.

9.title: Bulk-buy trade-off
9.desc: Checks whether a volume discount is worth it: weighs the savings against extra holding cost and the risk of stock expiring before it sells.

9.title: Remedy branch rebalancing
9.desc: Suggests moving stock between Remedy’s branches (BGC, Vertis North, Greenhills) to balance each site’s share and use up near-expiry stock. Remedy is a sister company and a customer; this is based on what Healthspan has shipped to them.

9.title: Data health
9.desc: A completeness check on the data behind every forecast — SKUs missing a price, expiry, batch, or bin, negative stock, and items with too little sales history. Fixing these in the source sheet sharpens the whole app.

9.title: Monthly movement
9.desc: Units received versus sold each month over the past year — the pulse of what’s coming in and going out.

9.title: Inventory value
9.desc: Where your inventory money sits, broken down by product line.

9.title: Deal scenarios
9.desc: What the current stock is worth if everything sells à la carte versus through the bundle deals (2+1 up to 6+1, where the +1 is free). Prices are live from Shopify where connected (sheet price otherwise).

9.title: Team & access
9.desc: Create, edit, and disable team accounts without opening Supabase. Add someone with a starter password, change roles and specialist tags, reset passwords, and disable accounts (kept, just blocked from signing in).
